fixes.answer: I see it as a genuinely [[double-edged]] phenomenon. On the positive side, it fosters greater understanding, tolerance and exchange between cultures, and lets us enjoy the best of what the world offers, from food to film. However, there is a real risk that it leads to cultural [[homogenisation]], where dominant cultures [[overwhelm]] local ones. So while I appreciate the connection it brings, I believe we must actively work to preserve cultural diversity alongside it.

The spread of English as a global [[lingua franca]] has clear benefits, facilitating international communication, business and science. However, it also poses a threat to [[linguistic diversity]]. As English dominates, some smaller languages are being [[marginalised]] and, in extreme cases, are dying out, taking unique cultural knowledge with them. So while a common language is enormously useful, its dominance risks a loss of the rich linguistic heritage that makes humanity so diverse.
fixes.why: 'linguistic heritage' split into plain marks; marked 'lingua franca' and 'linguistic diversity'

fixes.answer: Exposure to other cultures is generally very positive for people. It tends to make individuals more open-minded, tolerant and [[empathetic]], as they realise there are many valid ways of living. It challenges stereotypes and prejudices. It can also be creatively inspiring, blending ideas in new ways. So while it can occasionally cause a sense of confusion about one's own identity, overall I believe cultural exposure [[broadens horizons]] and [[enriches]] people enormously.
fixes.why: 'inspiring' is plain; marked 'empathetic' and the full phrase 'broadens horizons'

fixes.answer: There are several strategies. Governments can support and fund local arts, languages, film and traditions to ensure they thrive. Education that [[instils]] pride in one's heritage is fundamental. Protecting local media and industries from being entirely overwhelmed by [[global giants]] also helps. Crucially, this should be done not by rejecting outside influence, but by celebrating and promoting one's own culture so that it remains [[vibrant]] and valued.
fixes.why: 'promoting' and 'valued' are plain; marked 'instils' and 'global giants'

fixes.answer: The advantages are substantial: greater economic opportunity, the [[free flow of ideas]] and technology, cultural exchange, and international cooperation on shared problems. It has lifted many out of poverty. The disadvantages include cultural homogenisation, growing inequality, the exploitation of cheaper labour, and increased vulnerability to global crises, as the pandemic showed. So globalisation is a powerful force for connection and progress, but one with significant [[inequalities]] and [[vulnerabilities]].
fixes.why: 'connection' is plain; marked 'free flow of ideas'

fixes.answer: There is considerable truth to this, though it is not the whole picture. It is often argued that wealthy nations and large corporations reap the greatest rewards, while poorer countries may suffer exploitation and cultural erosion. The benefits are undeniably [[unevenly]] distributed. However, globalisation has arguably also lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty in developing nations. So while the [[playing field]] is far from level, I would not say the benefits are exclusively for the [[privileged]].
fixes.why: 'exclusively' is plain; marked 'playing field'; softened the poverty figure
